entities.summary:
Angola, officially the Republic of Angola, is a country on the western coast of Southern Africa. The seventh-largest country in Africa by area, with 36 million people, Angola is the second-largest Portuguese-speaking country after Brazil. Its vast reserves of oil (the second-largest in sub-Saharan Africa) and diamonds have generated enormous wealth that is extremely unequally distributed.

The Kongo Kingdom — centered at Mbanza Kongo (northern Angola) — was one of the most sophisticated pre-colonial states in Central Africa, with a centralized court, a system of taxation, and diplomatic relations with Portugal from 1483. Portuguese contact and the subsequent Atlantic slave trade devastated the region: Angola became the single largest source of enslaved Africans in the entire Atlantic slave trade — approximately 5.7 million people were forcibly shipped from Angolan ports between 1500 and 1850, primarily to Brazil.

Portuguese colonial rule was formalized in the late 19th century under the Berlin Conference (1884–85) and included brutal forced labor systems well into the 20th century. Angola's independence war (1961–1975) was followed immediately by a catastrophic civil war between MPLA (backed by Cuba and the Soviet Union) and UNITA (backed by the US and South Africa) that lasted 27 years (1975–2002) and killed over half a million people. Since 2002, oil-fueled economic growth has been dramatic but concentrated in an elite. Angola under the MPLA has never held a genuinely competitive election.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Kongo Kingdom's diplomatic relations with Portugal from 1483 and its subsequent devastation by the Atlantic slave trade had a profound impact on Angola's history, leading to the country becoming the single largest source of enslaved Africans in the entire Atlantic slave trade.
